html:
The criminal code of British India, passed in 1860 and in force from 1862. It stayed in force in independent India until 2024, and versions of it still serve in Pakistan, Bangladesh and other former colonies.

The first draft was written in the 1830s by a law commission led by Thomas Babington Macaulay. He wanted one clear written code for all of India in place of the mix of Hindu, Muslim and Company law then in use. The draft sat for decades; the shock of the Indian Rebellion of 1857 and the start of direct crown rule finally got it passed.

It defined crimes and punishments in plain, numbered sections with examples. Admired for its clarity, it was copied in Singapore, Malaysia, Burma, Sri Lanka and parts of Africa. Some sections were tools of empire: the sedition law, added in 1870, was used against nationalists including Gandhi. Section 377, against sex "against the order of nature", outlawed homosexuality until India's Supreme Court struck it down in 2018. In 2024 India replaced the code with a new law, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
